title: German noun genders & cases (intro)
examples: How do I know if a German noun is masculine or feminine?
What is the difference between the nominative and accusative case?
When do I use 'den' instead of 'der'?

explain.say: Today we are learning about German nouns and their genders. German nouns have three genders. These genders are masculine, feminine, and neuter.
The first gender is masculine, and we use the word der for it. For example, der Tisch means the table. The table is a masculine noun in German.
The second gender is feminine, and we use the word die for it. For example, die Lampe means the lamp. The lamp is a feminine noun in German.
The third gender is neuter, and we use the word das for it. For example, das Buch means the book. The book is a neuter noun in German.
Now we look at cases. The nominative case is for the subject of the sentence. The accusative case is for the direct object. Think of who is doing the action.
For example, the dog sees the ball. Here, the dog is the subject in the nominative case. The ball is what is seen, so it is in the accusative case.

faq.q: I keep mixing up der, die, and das. Is there a trick to remember which one to use?
faq.a: There is no single trick for every noun. You must learn the gender with the noun itself. Always learn the article with the word.
asks: How do I know the gender?
Is there a rule for der, die, das?

faq.q: When does a noun change from nominative to accusative? Does everything change?
faq.a: Only certain articles change between cases. For masculine nouns, der becomes den in the accusative case. Feminine and neuter articles usually stay the same.
asks: Does the case change the article?
What is the rule for case change?

faq.q: If I use the wrong article, will my sentence be completely wrong?
faq.a: Yes, using the wrong article can make the sentence incorrect. It shows that you do not know the noun's gender or case.
asks: Do I need to memorize all the articles?
What happens if I forget the article?

faq.q: What is the difference between the subject and the direct object in a sentence?
faq.a: The subject is the person or thing doing the action. The direct object is the person or thing receiving that action.
asks: What is the receiver of the action?

faq.q: Do all nouns have a gender?
faq.a: Yes, in German, almost all nouns have a grammatical gender. This gender is masculine, feminine, or neuter.

facts: German nouns are assigned one of three genders: masculine, feminine, or neuter.
The nominative case marks the subject of the sentence.
The accusative case marks the direct object that receives the action.
The masculine article changes from der in the nominative to den in the accusative.

quiz.say: If the cat (die Katze) chases the mouse (die Maus), which article is used for the mouse?
quiz.why: Since 'die Maus' is the direct object, and it is feminine, the article remains die.

wrong.1: This is wrong because 'den' is only used for masculine direct objects.
wrong.2: This is wrong because 'der' is used for the subject, not the object here.
wrong.3: This is wrong because 'das' is for neuter nouns, and 'Maus' is feminine.

quiz.say: The boy (der Junge) sees the ball (der Ball). Which article correctly marks the ball as the direct object?
quiz.why: The ball is masculine, and because it is the direct object, the article changes from der to den.

wrong.0: This is wrong because 'das' is used for neuter nouns.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the object requires the accusative case marker.
wrong.3: This is wrong because 'die' is only used for feminine nouns.
